entities.description:
Read the stacked notation as n choose k, not n divided by k. We choose which trial positions are positive, not the order in which those positions are selected.
For ten trials and two positives, select two distinct positions; the other eight are negative. Choosing positions 2 then 7 gives the same positive-position set as choosing 7 then 2. Different positive-position sets give different binary sequences.
In the binomial probability formula each such sequence has the same probability under independent trials with a common success probability. The coefficient counts the sequences; it is not itself a probability.
entities.label: l5 choose explain1

entities.description:
There are ten choices for the first position and nine for the second, giving 90 ordered pairs. Each unordered pair appears twice, so divide by two to obtain 45.
Factorials give the same calculation: expand 10! down to 8! and cancel 8!. The denominator 2! equals two times one.
Choosing no positions or all positions each gives exactly one selection. The convention zero factorial equals one makes the general formula valid at both boundaries, including n equal to zero. All counts and probabilities here are dimensionless; the count 45 is not 45 percent.
entities.label: l5 choose explain2

entities.description: Factorial multiplies the positive whole numbers up to its argument. Thus 2! is two times one. By convention 0! equals one. Parentheses make n minus k the factorial argument.

entities.label: l5 choose operators

entities.description: For whole numbers n at least zero and k between zero and n, count selections of k distinct positions, without replacement and without regard to selection order. entities.description: An F variable is the ratio of two independent chi-square variables, each divided by its own degrees of freedom. For two independent samples, each iid normal, the sample-variance ratio has an F reference under equal population variances, with numerator sample size minus one and denominator sample size minus one degrees of freedom, in that order. An observed ratio alone does not establish different population precisions. The classical variance comparison is sensitive to nonnormality.

entities.description: The method SDs are constructed 0.20 and 0.40 mg/L. They supply a descriptive variance ratio of 4 but no sample sizes, sampling design or evidence of normality. Do not attach a p value, critical value or formal decision to them. The separate theoretical F density chooses numerator degrees of freedom 10 and denominator 5 only to illustrate the law. If this were a normal-sample variance-ratio application, these would correspond to sample sizes 11 in the numerator and 6 in the denominator, but those sizes are not asserted for A and B. The density at nonnegative dimensionless x is (a/b)^(a/2) times x^(a/2-1) divided by Beta(a/2,b/2), times (1+a*x/b)^(-(a+b)/2), with a=10 and b=5. Beta(p,q) is Gamma(p)*Gamma(q)/Gamma(p+q). Coordinates are theoretical, rounded to twelve decimals, and connected linearly for drawing. Support extends to infinity and the 0 to 8 display is not renormalized. A separate deterministic arithmetic illustration chooses U1=16, nu1=10, U2=2, nu2=5, giving normalized components 1.6 and 0.4 and ratio 4. These are not simulated draws, independent evidence, or measurements from either method. The construction assumes independent chi-square variables at the distributional level; one chosen quotient does not demonstrate that distribution.

Constructed classifications of 100 independently sampled particles under a hypothetical iid categorical model, not measured field data and not the five KS readings. Diameter bands are [0,5), [5,10), [10,20), [20,40) and [40,infinity) micrometres. Diameters are nonnegative; each lower boundary is included and each finite upper boundary excluded. Thus 5 belongs to the second band, and all diameters at least 40 stay in the last band. The five bands are fixed before observing counts.

Null probabilities are fixed at 0.10, 0.20, 0.40, 0.20 and 0.10. Expected counts are 10,20,40,20,10. Observed counts 4,12,44,24,16 sum to the same fixed total 100. No probability is fitted to these data. Pearson contributions are 3.6,3.2,0.4,0.8,3.6, sum 11.6. The first observed count is only 4 but its expected count is 10; the approximation check concerns expectations. Zero observed counts would still contribute when expectations are positive. Zero null probability with a positive observed count is a null-impossible event, not a denominator to divide by; structurally impossible zero-probability categories require separate handling.

Under this fixed multinomial null, the reference converges to chi-square with k-1=4 degrees of freedom as total size increases. It is not the exact normal-sample variance identity from T16. The chosen 5% reference cutoff is 9.487729036781154. The chi-square-four survival function at nonnegative q is exp(-q/2)*(1+q/2). It gives 0.05 at that cutoff and 0.020587372268555542 at Q=11.6. These are exact calculations for the reference distribution, but its application to this finite multinomial sample is approximate. Reject the specified category-probability null at the prespecified nominal 5% level using this approximation. No exact finite-sample multinomial p value is claimed. A p value is not the probability that the null is true or false.

For fitted categorical models, a k-1-m reference requires appropriate regular estimation of m identifiable parameters, usually from the grouped multinomial likelihood, with sufficient positive expected counts and positive remaining degrees of freedom. Estimation from ungrouped observations, adaptive categories or other fitting schemes does not automatically justify subtracting m. Use an appropriately calibrated method or simulate the whole analysis, including fitting and any category-selection rule. A prespecified pooling scheme based on expected counts changes the category count and must be reflected in the reference. Do not drop empty observed categories or tail bins, or choose bins after inspecting departures to optimize a result. Independence, fixed category definitions and representative sampling are substantive assumptions. Pearson loses within-class location information; grouped counts cannot reconstruct the raw observations or the KS statistic. The positive and negative discrepancies show which bands differ descriptively, but global rejection does not identify a unique alternative model or a cause such as contamination or measurement bias.

entities.description: A predefined rule turns the signal into positive or negative. False positives and false negatives remain possible; negative does not prove absence.

A finding is not the true sample state

entities.description: A positive analytical finding is a decision about a signal, not an infallible statement of the true sample state. In a specified target population, observed positive-result probability combines sensitivity among true positives and false-positive probability among true negatives, weighted by their population proportions. It is generally different from true prevalence and from detection probability at a fixed concentration. Homogeneous test-performance probabilities are a teaching assumption, not a guarantee across concentrations, matrices or sampling schemes.
entities.label: l5 v02 definition

entities.description: Hypothetical homogeneous screening-performance model, not measured PFAS prevalence or a validated assay specification. Define true positivity by one chosen scientific target condition and a suitable reference standard. Target-population true prevalence is 0.01, sensitivity 0.90 and false-positive rate 0.05. Then false-negative rate is 0.10 and specificity 0.95. By the law of total probability, marginal positive-finding probability is 0.01*0.90 + 0.99*0.05 = 0.0585. For 10,000 randomly selected samples, expected true-positive/false-negative/false-positive/true-negative classification counts are 90/10/495/9405. These are model expectations, not an observed confusion matrix or guaranteed allocation. Total expected positives 585 and negatives 9415; total true positives 100 and true negatives 9900. Among the expected positive findings, the ratio 90/585 is about 15.38%; that is distinct from sensitivity, whose denominator is all truly positive samples. No new formula for predictive value is needed in this first reserve increment. The conditional test-performance groups have different denominators. Marginal positive counts can follow a binomial model only with a fixed number of independent units and common positive-result probability. The mixture identity for one randomly selected unit itself does not require independence across units. For repeat readings at a fixed concentration, detection probability depends on that concentration, procedure and matrix, not on an environmental-population prevalence. No legal threshold, method-performance claim, real prevalence estimate or deconvolution of prevalence from observed positivity is asserted.
entities.label: l5 v02 model

entities.description: Teaching assumptions: prevalence 1%, sensitivity 90%, false-positive rate 5%. Positive-result probability: 5.85%, not 1%.

entities.description: Positive-result probability equals true prevalence times sensitivity plus true-negative prevalence times false-positive rate. Here 0.01 times 0.90 plus 0.99 times 0.05 gives 0.0585, or 5.85%.

entities.description: Multiply adjacent factors, add the two disjoint routes; subtract from 1 for the complement. All quantities are dimensionless probabilities. Fixed homogeneous performance is assumed.

entities.description: Se: positive finding given true positive, 0.90. FPR: positive finding given true negative, 0.05. Denominators are different true-state groups.

entities.description: At a fixed concentration, independent repeat classifications under stable conditions can be modelled by a binomial count with a common concentration-specific positive-finding probability. A logistic relation between concentration and log odds is one possible model family, not a physical law or evidence of analytical performance. The unit, concentration coding, matrix, preparation and calibration range must be specified; detection probability at fixed concentration is not target-population prevalence.

entities.description: A separate specified teaching model, not a calibration of V02's sensitivity or false-positive rate. Concentration c is nonnegative and uses mg/L. The chosen dimensionless log-odds intercept is -4 and slope is 2 L/mg. Positive-finding probability is 1/(1+exp(4-2*c)) when c is expressed numerically in mg/L. The illustrative display covers 0 to 4 mg/L; it is not an experimentally validated calibration range. At c=0 the model gives about 0.017986, at c=1 about 0.119203, at c=2 exactly 0.5, at c=3 about 0.880797 and at c=4 about 0.982014. The nonzero zero-concentration probability is an illustrative baseline finding rate; no real false-positive performance is inferred. At 2 mg/L, ten independent decisions with common probability 0.5 give exact binomial count masses choose(10,k)/1024 for k=0 through 10, mean count 5 and variance 2.5. An expected count of 5 is not a fixed allocation in every realized run. No observations, simulation or parameter fit are claimed. Logistic drawing coordinates are rounded to twelve decimal places and joined linearly; no raw-observation markers are shown. The natural logarithm acts on dimensionless odds. Changing concentration units or centering/coding requires a matching parameter transformation; slope cannot retain its numerical value under arbitrary recoding. A fitted curve requires independent evidence, uncertainty assessment, matrix/preparation scope and a justified observation model. Correlated repeats, changing concentration, varying preparation or drift can violate the simple binomial assumptions. The 50% probability midpoint is not automatically an analytical detection limit or a legal decision threshold. No method validation or environmental prevalence claim is made.

Divide by n−1; define sample variance

entities.description:
The individual residual is dᵢ = Xᵢ − X̄. The common shift is Δ = X̄ − μ. Their sum gives Xᵢ − μ.
Square each side, then use the binomial identity with a = dᵢ and b = Δ.
Squaring an equality gives a consequence; sign information would be needed to reverse squaring in general.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 1

entities.description:
Sum the observation-wise equality from i = 1 to n.
Distribute the sum over all three terms. In the general rule use aᵢ = dᵢ², bᵢ = dᵢ, c = 2Δ and q = Δ².
The coefficient 2Δ is common to every observation, so it moves outside the cross-term sum. Keep the last sum explicit for now.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 2

entities.description:
These residuals were formed about their own sample arithmetic mean. Their sum is exactly zero.
Substituting Σdᵢ = 0 makes the entire cross term 2ΔΣdᵢ equal to zero.
The individual residuals and their squared sum are not zero. Only the signed residual sum vanishes.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 3

entities.description:
Within one sample, Δ = X̄ − μ does not depend on the observation index i. Its square is therefore also index-independent.
Use c = Δ² in the rule for summing a constant: the same value is added n times.
Δ is still random across repeated samples. Being constant with respect to i does not make it fixed across samples.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 4

entities.description:
Now pass from a within-sample identity to a statement about repeated sampling.
Take expectations on both sides and use linearity on the residual-square sum plus the shared-shift term.
Finite variance makes the required expectations finite. Independence is needed for later sample-mean moments, not for linearity itself.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 5

entities.description:
About the fixed population mean, each observation has expected squared deviation σ². The finite sum therefore has expectation nσ².
Use the separately established auxiliary result E[nΔ²] = σ² for the shared-shift term.
These substitutions rely on the sampling assumptions and the preceding auxiliary result, not on algebra alone.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 6

entities.description:
In the general rearrangement use a = nσ², b = E[Σdᵢ²] and c = σ².
Subtract σ² from both sides. The difference nσ² − σ² factors as (n−1)σ².
This step is algebraic once the preceding statistical moment results have been established.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 7

entities.description:
The expected residual sum of squares is (n−1)σ². Divide the statistic by the fixed positive count n−1.
Use c = 1/(n−1) in linearity of expectation, then define that normalized statistic as s². Its expectation is σ².
In contrast, dividing by n gives the descriptive MSD, whose expectation is (n−1)σ²/n. This does not make descriptive MSD erroneous. Residual degrees of freedom are a separate constraint argument; the square root s is not automatically unbiased.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 8

entities.description: Xᵢ: random observation i; X̄: sample mean; μ: population mean; dᵢ = Xᵢ − X̄; Δ = X̄ − μ. Lowercase xᵢ, x̄ are realized values.
entities.label: Observations and centers

entities.description: n > 1: count; i: index; Σ: sum from 1 to n. E: expectation; Var: variance; σ²: population variance; s²: sample variance.
entities.label: Counts and moments

entities.description: a, b, c, q: scalar placeholders; aᵢ, bᵢ: indexed terms. U, V, Y: random quantities. A constant moved outside Σ or E is fixed for that operation.
entities.label: General rule placeholders

entities.description:
The individual residual dᵢ measures Xᵢ from its sample mean X̄. The shared shift Δ measures that mean from μ.
Substitute both definitions into dᵢ + Δ. The terms −X̄ and +X̄ cancel, leaving Xᵢ − μ. In the general identity, a = Xᵢ, b = X̄, c = μ.
This is an algebraic consequence of the definitions, with no normality or independence assumption. Δ is common to the indices within a sample, but can vary across samples.
entities.label: md centers explanation
Substitute dᵢ and Δ; cancel X̄

entities.description:
Use the five observed experiment sums: 10, 13, 18, 10 and 23. The count n is 5.
Adding gives 74; division by 5 gives 14.8. These are observed experiment sums, not the population expectation of a die.
Normality is not needed to compute this finite arithmetic mean.
entities.label: md mean reference explanation
Insert the five observations; add and divide
Use variance about the expected mean
Multiply the expectation by fixed n

entities.description:
For iid observations with finite variance, the sample mean has expectation μ and variance σ²/n. These are the required auxiliary moment results, not a new topic about confidence intervals.
Insert Y = X̄ into the variance definition. Because E(X̄) = μ, the expected squared shift from μ equals Var(X̄).
Uppercase X̄ denotes the random sample mean; lowercase x̄ denotes a realized value.
entities.label: md shift explanation 1

entities.description: erf is the special error function, not an inverse function or a probability. Lowercase u is its dimensionless argument; t is a dimensionless dummy integration variable, reused independently in each integral. The integral runs from zero to u and dt identifies its integration variable. e is the base of the natural exponential; minus t squared is its exponent. Pi is the circle constant; square roots are positive. The factor two divided by the square root of pi normalizes erf. In the CDF identity, divide standardized threshold z by the square root of two, evaluate erf, add one and multiply by one half; parentheses and square brackets group these operations. All arguments, integrals and function values here are dimensionless. Phi is an antiderivative of the standard-normal density phi; the displayed lower limit minus infinity fixes its probability normalization. There is no elementary antiderivative of the Gaussian density. erf supplies a special-function representation, not a new distributional assumption.

Uppercase Z subscript n: dimensionless standardized random total, still discrete for finite n; lowercase z would denote one realized value. Juxtaposition multiplies; subtract, divide and take positive roots as shown; equals rewrites identities, tilde names the law.

Standard-normal N(0,1) has mean zero and variance one. Phi lowercase is standard-normal density; f with subscript X is concentration density in L/mg. The factor one over sigma changes density units. entities.description: X: random individual nitrate result, not a mean; x: concentration coordinate; a and b: ordered bounds, all in mg/L. P: probability; less-than-or-equal includes endpoints, which have zero point probability for this density model. f(x): model density in L/mg, not a histogram height. The integral adds density times infinitesimal concentration increments dx from a to b. Area is unitless. F: cumulative probability; subtract its lower value from its upper value. Equals links the same event. Density is nonnegative with total area one.

entities.description: A cumulative distribution adds probability up to a threshold. Observed cumulative fractions estimate it; the population model is not the sample.

entities.description: Nitrate illustration: 1,000 simulated results under a stated model, not laboratory measurements. The smooth curve is a model PDF. Narrow the selected interval and compare area, not height. The bounded flat alternative shows that the tools are not specific to a bell curve.

entities.description: X: random concentration; x: threshold, both mg/L. F(x)=P(X at most x): unitless cumulative probability. For an absolutely continuous model, integrate density f(t) in L/mg from negative infinity to x. t is a dummy concentration coordinate; dt is its infinitesimal increment. Minus infinity means no finite lower bound, not negative probability. The prime differentiates with respect to x; the slope equals f where this derivative relation holds, not automatically at density discontinuities. Equals links the expressions. Every distribution has a CDF; not every distribution has a PDF.

entities.description: Simulation, not laboratory measurements: hold model expectation 10.00 mg/L and SD 0.10 mg/L fixed. Grow the sample from 20 to 1,000. entities.description: Two constructed teaching samples, each n=5, are compared with a normal model fixed before either sample: mean 10 mg/L, SD 0.50 mg/L. A: 9.4, 9.8, 10.0, 10.2, 10.6 mg/L. B: 10.3, 10.31, 10.32, 10.33, 12.0 mg/L, a deliberately right-skewed departure. Neither set proves a population family. Q-Q probabilities are (i-0.5)/5 for sorted rank i. Corresponding normal quantiles are 9.3592242172277, 9.73779974364598, 10.0, 10.26220025635402, 10.6407757827723 mg/L. For KS check both jump sides, not just included ECDF values. A has D=0.14457825838967642; B has D=0.7257468822499269 at the left side of the first jump (10.3 mg/L). Both use exact n=5 two-sided fixed-continuous-null cutoff 0.5632751983660635 at alpha 0.05. A is not rejected, B is rejected. The figures use the same samples for both Q-Q and KS, but visual compatibility is not proof of normality. If parameters are fitted to these data, use suitable Lilliefors or refitted-bootstrap calibration instead of this classical table. Fixed affine transformation of both data and model preserves KS distance. Standardizing with estimated parameters does not restore classical calibration.

entities.description: An integrable random quantity in an expectation identity.
entities.label: rule U symbol

entities.description: A second integrable random quantity.
entities.label: rule V symbol

entities.description: A random quantity with the moments required by the stated identity.
entities.label: rule Y symbol

entities.description: A placeholder quantity or indexed term in a general mathematical identity.
entities.label: rule a symbol

entities.description: Arithmetic mean of the same finite values a_i.
entities.label: rule abar symbol

entities.description: Insert the two defined differences. Adding them makes the intermediate value appear once with a minus sign and once with a plus sign, so it cancels.
entities.label: Substitute and cancel the intermediate center

entities.description: For n numerical observations, add the values and divide their sum by the positive count n.
entities.label: Arithmetic mean

entities.description: A second placeholder quantity or indexed term.
entities.label: rule b symbol

entities.description: Multiplying a+b by itself gives a², the two equal cross-products ab, and b². Squaring both sides of an equality is a valid implication, not generally a reversible operation without sign information.
entities.label: Binomial square

entities.description: A scalar placeholder; a fixed constant when pulled outside a sum or expectation.
entities.label: rule c symbol

entities.description: If every indexed quantity has expectation m and variance v, the sums of these expectations and variances are nm and nv. This is substitution followed by summing a constant. It says nothing by itself about the variance of a sum: that separate operation may need covariance terms.
entities.label: Substitute common moments in a finite sum

entities.description: Covariance of two random quantities; it measures their joint linear variation.
entities.label: rule cov symbol

entities.description: For U and V with finite second moments, covariance is the expected product of their centered deviations. Positive covariance indicates joint movement in the same direction, negative covariance opposing movement. Independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance does not generally imply independence.
entities.label: Covariance definition

entities.description: Take expectations of equal integrable random quantities and distribute E over addition. Independence of the two summands is not needed for linearity.
entities.label: Linearity of expectation

entities.description: For integrable random quantities U and V, expectation distributes over their sum. A fixed coefficient c may be taken outside E. Independence is not needed for this rule.
entities.label: Linearity with a fixed multiplier

entities.description: A constant has the same value on every repetition. Its probability-weighted theoretical average is therefore that value. This is not a statement about a random observation that happens to be observed once.
entities.label: Expected value of a constant

entities.description: If integrable random quantities agree with probability one, their expectations agree. Applying E does not require independence. An equality between expectations alone does not recover equality of the random quantities, so the displayed direction is an implication.
entities.label: Expectation preserves equality

entities.description: A constant fixed across repeated samples multiplies the expectation. A random offset such as Δ must not itself be pulled outside E; the fixed count n may be.
entities.label: Factor a fixed constant out of expectation

entities.description: The sample count is fixed and positive. Move 1/n outside expectation and distribute expectation over the finite sum. This needs finite expectations, not independence. It applies to observations and also to squared deviations when their expectations exist.
entities.label: Expected value of a finite average

entities.description: For a fixed finite number of integrable random quantities, apply expectation addition repeatedly. E[ΣY_i] = ΣE[Y_i]. Neither independence nor identical distribution is required. This finite-sum rule alone does not justify interchanging an infinite sum and expectation.
entities.label: Expectation of a finite sum

entities.description: For an integrable random variable Y and fixed real a and b, multiplying the variable by a multiplies its expectation by a; adding b shifts the expectation by b. No independence assumption is needed because the other terms are constants.
entities.label: Expectation under scaling and translation

entities.description: Write a as na/n, subtract a/n and factor out a. The result holds for every real a and positive integer n. This is algebra, not an additional statistical assumption.
entities.label: Factor a common value

entities.description: Split the finite sum over subtraction, count c exactly n times, and substitute Σa_i = n ā. This needs the arithmetic mean of those same values and does not require probability assumptions.
entities.label: Sum distances from a fixed center

entities.description: For independent integrable quantities, the joint distribution factors and the expectation of the product is the product of the expectations. This is not linearity and is generally false for dependent quantities. The independence assumption also ensures integrability of the product under the stated finite absolute moments.
entities.label: Expectation of an independent product

entities.description: The indexed random quantity i in a finite sum.
entities.label: rule indexed Y symbol

entities.description: Subtract c from both sides and read the equality in reverse. This is an equivalent algebraic rearrangement.
entities.label: Subtract the same term

entities.description: Fixed coefficients and a random quantity.
entities.label: Affine expectation

entities.description: Two integrable random quantities.
entities.label: Expectation addition

entities.description: Finite variance and two fixed scalars.
entities.label: Affine variance

entities.description: Expectation and a fixed constant.
entities.label: Constant

entities.description: Both quantities have finite second moments.
entities.label: Variance and covariance

entities.description: A positive count of independent finite-variance quantities.
entities.label: Finite independent sum

entities.description: Independent quantities with finite second moments.
entities.label: Independent pair

entities.description: Finite variance and fixed coefficients.
entities.label: Variance transformation

entities.description: Common expectation of the indexed quantities.
entities.label: rule m symbol

entities.description: Expand each centered difference, distribute the finite sum, and use Σ(a_i−c) = n(ā−c). The two cross-term contributions combine with the last squared shift to leave one negative squared shift. The fitted mean removes a nonnegative term. This is an exact algebraic identity for each realization, not an expectation or an unbiasedness claim.
entities.label: Center squared distances at their arithmetic mean

entities.description: Multiplying the definition of the arithmetic mean by the positive count n gives the sum of the observations.
entities.label: Use the arithmetic mean

entities.description: Divide both sides by the same positive n. Subtract c from both sides to isolate the normalized b term. These are reversible algebraic operations and require no probability assumptions.
entities.label: Divide by a fixed count and rearrange

entities.description: Each observation has expected squared deviation σ² about μ. A finite sum gives nσ². The previously established sample-mean calculation gives E[nΔ²] = σ².
entities.label: Insert the established moment results

entities.description: A factor that does not depend on the index multiplies the entire sum.
entities.label: Factor a constant out of a sum

entities.description: A separate index-independent term; it need not be the square of another coefficient.
entities.label: rule q symbol

entities.description: Subtracting the fitted arithmetic mean from every observation creates one exact sum constraint. It is a deterministic identity, not a claim about expectation.
entities.label: Residuals sum to zero

entities.description: Fixed real scale factor in an affine transformation.
entities.label: rule scale symbol

entities.description: Expand E[(Y−E[Y])²] and use linearity. The middle term is −2(E[Y])² and the constant term is (E[Y])². Rearranging gives E[Y²] = Var(Y)+(E[Y])². A finite second moment is required; independence is not.
entities.label: Second moment and variance

entities.description: Fixed real additive shift in an affine transformation.
entities.label: rule shift symbol

entities.description: Insert an already established equality into the expression, then factor the common value. The statistical premises of the inserted result remain necessary; this algebra does not establish them.
entities.label: Substitute and factor the fixed count

entities.description: Equal values may replace one another in the same expression whenever the operations are defined. The mathematical justification of the substituted value must have been established first; substitution does not prove a statistical premise.
entities.label: Substitute an established equality

entities.description: First distribute the sum over a difference. The second sum repeats c exactly n times and equals nc.
entities.label: Split a sum and count the constant

entities.description: The same value is added once for each of n indices. A quantity can be random across samples and still be constant with respect to i within a given sample.
entities.label: Sum a constant

entities.description: Add the left sides and the right sides of equalities that hold at every index. This gives a consequence; the summed equality alone does not recover every individual equality.
entities.label: Sum indexed equalities

entities.description: A finite sum distributes over addition. No independence or probability assumption is needed.
entities.label: Linearity of a finite sum

entities.description: Use linearity for each of the three summands and move the index-independent coefficient c outside the middle sum. The last sum is not simplified yet.
entities.label: Distribute the sum and factor the cross term

entities.description: Common finite variance of the indexed quantities.
entities.label: rule v symbol

entities.description: For a fixed real constant c, E[c] = c, so c−E[c] = 0 on every outcome. Its expected squared centered deviation is therefore zero.
entities.label: Variance of a constant

entities.description: For two random quantities with finite second moments, expand the squared centered sum. The expected cross product is the covariance. Positive covariance increases the variance of the sum; negative covariance decreases it. Independence is not needed for this identity.
entities.label: Variance-covariance identity

entities.description: For a random variable with finite second moment, variance is the expected squared distance from its expectation.
entities.label: Variance is an expected squared deviation

entities.description: Mutual independence makes every cross covariance zero. The variance of the finite sum then equals the sum of its variances. For two variables this reduces to Var(U+V) = Var(U)+Var(V). Standard deviations are not directly additive.
entities.label: Variance of a finite independent sum

entities.description: Combine translation invariance with the squared scaling factor. For fixed a and b and finite variance, Var(aY+b) = a² Var(Y). Unlike expectation, variance does not acquire an additive b term.
entities.label: Variance under scaling and translation

entities.description: Variance squares the centered distance. Replacing Y by cY multiplies every centered distance by c and its square by c². Consequently variance is multiplied by c², not by c. The standard deviation is multiplied by the absolute value of c.
entities.label: Variance under scaling

entities.description: Adding a fixed c moves the random quantity and its expectation by the same amount. Their difference is unchanged, so the variance is unchanged. This does not hold for adding an arbitrary random quantity.
entities.label: Variance under translation

entities.description: For a finite collection with finite second moments, the variance-covariance identity includes all pairwise cross covariances. When each is zero, only the individual variances remain. Independence is sufficient for this result but pairwise zero covariance is enough.
entities.label: Variance of a pairwise uncorrelated sum

entities.description: Illustrative nitrate IC data, n=20. Heights are relative-frequency density in L/mg; bin area is an observed fraction. All readings remain included when bins move. This is not a fitted normal PDF.

entities.description: Standard deviation is the non-negative square root of a variance. entities.description: RSS is sum of squared response residuals in squared response units. Subscripts s and c denote simple linear and complex quadratic models on identical observations. p counts all fitted coefficients including intercept: p s=2 and p c=3. n=12 is count. Subtract RSS for added-term SS, divide by added df p c minus p s=1; divide complex RSS by residual df n minus p c=9. Their ratio F is unitless. Under H subscript zero (quadratic coefficient zero), tilde names F law with ordered df 1,9. Minus, division and equality are arithmetic; comma orders df. Normal iid errors with common positive variance, fixed predictor values and full-rank nested designs give the exact reference.
entities.label: tf cal law symbol
Which two quadratic forms supply the F law?
Fit both models to the same twelve points

entities.description: Twelve fixed concentrations from 0 to 10 mg/L, with synthetic response in arbitrary units. Fit intercept plus concentration, then add squared concentration. On the same data, nested ordinary least squares cannot increase residual sum of squares when a term is added.

entities.description: A smaller RSS alone does not justify curvature. Compare improvement per added parameter with remaining error variance. The null says the quadratic coefficient is zero. Assume fixed error-free concentrations and independent normal, equal-variance response errors; other calibration designs require other analyses.

entities.description: The 10.00 mg/L reference is just inside. In repeated iid normal studies, 95% of intervals from this procedure cover the fixed true mean. This is not a 95% probability assigned to the mean after observing this particular interval, nor a range for 95% of individual readings.

entities.description: Bar x=10.10 mg/L and s=0.10 mg/L are observed mean and sample SD; n=6 is count. t with subscript 0.975 semicolon 5 is the dimensionless 97.5th percentile 2.57058 of Student t with five df. Divide s by positive root n for estimated SE, multiply by the quantile for margin 0.10494 mg/L. Plus/minus forms lower and upper endpoints; brackets and comma delimit the closed interval; equality gives rounded endpoints. mg/L is milligrams per litre. The confidence level is 95%, matching a two-sided 5% test under the same model.
entities.label: tf ci symbol

entities.description: For iid normal results, the standardized mean and the scaled sample variance are independent. This independence is essential: an arbitrary normal numerator divided by a correlated variance estimate need not have a t distribution.
entities.label: tf construction

entities.description: n is count, nu=n minus one is df (5 here). S squared is random sample variance with divisor n minus one; sigma squared is fixed true variance, both in (mg/L) squared. Q is their unitless scaled ratio; chi squared names the chi-square law, subscript nu gives df. Z is the mean minus true mu divided by sigma over root n, an independent standard normal. Bar X and mu are in mg/L; S is sample SD in mg/L. Dividing by positive root Q over nu defines unitless T. Squaring, subtraction, multiplication and division have their usual arithmetic meanings; equality defines quantities, tilde names their laws. Lowercase t with subscript nu names the Student law, not an observed value. For a null test replace mu by mu subscript zero under that null.
entities.label: tf construction symbol

entities.description: Lowercase t is the observed unitless statistic, bar x=10.10 is the observed mean, mu subscript zero=10.00 the null reference, and s=0.10 the sample SD, in mg/L. n=6 is sample size. Subtraction gives the mean departure; division by s over positive root n uses estimated SE 0.040825 mg/L. Equal signs give the calculation; approximately allows rounding. This t is not a density or a probability.

F combines two independent chi-square quantities

entities.description: Under equal population variances the unknown common variance cancels, leaving the random sample-variance ratio B/A. Each group is iid normal and the groups are independent. Equal group means are not required.

entities.description: Index j is A or B; nu subscript j is that group's sample count minus one. S squared is its random sample variance and sigma squared its positive true variance, in (mg/L) squared. Multiply variance by df and divide by true variance to obtain unitless Q, a chi-square variable. Q A and Q B are independent. Divide each by its own df, then take B over A. F denotes the resulting unitless variable and, on the right, the F distribution name. Its first df is numerator B, second denominator A; both five here. Squares mean variance; equality defines quantities, tilde names laws, comma orders parameters. Without equal variances the observed sample ratio must also be divided by the true B/A variance ratio to have this reference law.
entities.label: tf f law symbol

entities.description:

entities.label: tf known

entities.description: Bar X is the random sample mean; mu is the population mean; mu subscript zero is the null reference 10.00, all in mg/L. Sigma is fixed positive individual SD in mg/L, n=6 is the count. Square means variance; division by n gives mean variance, positive square root n gives SE. Subtract and divide define unitless Z. Tilde means distributed as; N lists mean then variance. H subscript zero assumes mu equals the reference. Only then does Z have mean zero and variance one; comma separates parameters and equality defines the statistic.

Independent groups, not paired rows; concentrations in mg/L

entities.description: A retains mean 10.10 and SD 0.10 mg/L. B has mean 10.00 and SD 0.30 mg/L. B's observed mean is closer to the CRM, while A's observed spread is smaller. Trueness and precision are different properties; six results do not establish either population property.
entities.label: tf ratio

entities.description: Lowercase f is the observed dimensionless ratio. Lowercase s squared means sample variance computed about each group's own mean, using divisor five. Subscripts B and A identify the devices; values 0.090 and 0.010 are in (mg/L) squared, so units cancel on division. Equality gives arithmetic results. B/A is assigned before inspecting the data; never automatically put the larger estimate on top. Each group has six results, independent within and between groups.
entities.label: tf ratio symbol
Compare variance estimates, not the means

entities.description: Squaring an independent standard-normal numerator gives chi-square with one df. Squaring removes the sign: the two-sided t event becomes one upper-tail F event. Do not double this F tail again. This is not the two-device F ratio 9 with df 5,5.
entities.label: tf square

entities.description: T is a random Student variable; Z is standard normal, independent of chi-square Q with nu df. Superscript two squares a variable. Divide Q by positive df nu (five here). Z squared has chi-square df one, so the ratio has F law with numerator df one and denominator df nu; tilde means distributed as. Lowercase t is observed root six; its square is six. p is the upper-tail probability 0.05797 under F with df 1,5, equal to the two-sided t-five p-value. All quantities are dimensionless; equals gives identities or rounded calculations, comma separates ordered df.
entities.label: tf square symbol
Square a t variable and obtain an F variable
Repeated means with known versus estimated SE

entities.description:
Six minutes: calculate mean, variance, SD and the count within the illustrative 9.5–10.5 mg/L interval (endpoints included).
Does the smaller observed SD support better precision for A under these conditions? What can five results not establish about trueness or long-term performance? Means and SDs are in mg/L; variances are in (mg/L)².
entities.label: v23 task

entities.description: Interpret RSD only for a suitable ratio-scale quantity: ratios and an absolute zero must be meaningful, and the mean must be sufficiently separated from zero for the purpose. For positive concentrations, the RSD ratio equals CV = s/x̄.
entities.label: Relative Standard Deviation

entities.description: Relative standard deviation is the dimensionless ratio of sample standard deviation to the magnitude of the sample mean. Multiplying the ratio by one hundred gives its numerical percentage value.
entities.label: v24 formula

entities.description: The bars mean absolute value. Our concentration means are positive. A nonzero denominator alone does not guarantee a scientifically useful ratio.
entities.label: |x̄|: nonzero mean magnitude

entities.description: A ratio of 0.02 is 2%. Multiplication by 100 changes the numerical reporting scale, not the physical dimension.
entities.label: 100: report the ratio as percent

entities.description: Absolute spread in the same unit as the sample mean. The units cancel in their ratio: RSD is dimensionless.
entities.label: s: sample SD

entities.description: For these five repeats, B's relative spread is about 6.37 times A's. This compares sample dispersion under the stated conditions, not trueness or guaranteed long-term performance.
entities.label: RSD in Analytical Quality Control

entities.description: A
entities.label: v25 a1

entities.description: B
entities.label: v25 b1

entities.description: RSD expresses SD as a percentage of the concentration level rather than in mg/L.
entities.label: v25 key

entities.description: Both means are 10 mg/L: the SD and RSD rankings are identical, not independent evidence.
entities.label: v25 key2

entities.description: Compute from unrounded SDs. Display SD to three decimals and RSD to two; both SDs use n − 1 = 4.
entities.label: v25 key3

entities.description: A: about 1.58%; B: about 10.07%. Both use the sample SD with n − 1 = 4.
entities.label: Same center, different relative spread

entities.description: The mean and SD both increase tenfold, so their ratio stays constant: RSD = 2%. Equal relative spread does not mean equal absolute spread. Such comparisons still require a compatible quantity, meaningful zero and relevant measurement conditions.
entities.label: Absolute vs Relative Spread

entities.description: Illustrative summaries: identical bar heights show equal RSD, while the table shows different absolute SDs.
entities.label: Same relative spread at different levels

entities.description: Derived summaries for two illustrative levels, not individual measured observations: 100 times 0.2/10 and 100 times 2/100 both equal 2 percent.
entities.label: v26 rsd data

entities.description: Even on a concentration scale with a meaningful zero, a blank mean near zero is a poor denominator. Blank-corrected estimates may be positive or negative. Celsius temperature has a different problem: its arbitrary zero makes RSD inappropriate regardless of the denominator's size.
entities.label: When RSD Is Misleading

entities.description: Mean = 0.001 mg/L; SD = 0.020 mg/L. RSD = 2000%, driven by a tiny denominator.
entities.label: Illustrative blank

entities.description: Division by zero: RSD is undefined, not zero. Near zero it is unstable and can change drastically.
entities.label: Exactly zero mean

entities.description: Ratios require a meaningful zero. Absolute values in the denominator do not repair arbitrary scale origins.
entities.label: Check the measurement scale

entities.description: undefined
entities.label: v27 e3

entities.description: Hold absolute SD fixed at 0.020 mg/L. Only the illustrative mean changes.
entities.label: v27 k1

entities.description: At a zero mean, RSD is undefined; near zero it is unstable. Taking an absolute value does not fix this.
entities.label: v27 k2

entities.description: A huge RSD alone does not prove a poor method. For blanks, assess absolute SD and the relevant detection or decision requirements.
entities.label: v27 k3

entities.description:
Compare n = 3 and n = 30 from the same iid normal population: μ = 10 mg/L, σ = 2 mg/L.
Sample variance is unbiased: E[s²] = 4 (mg/L)². Sample SD is generally not unbiased for σ.
Monte Carlo means approximate expectations; SD percentiles describe repeated estimates, not a confidence interval for σ from one sample.
entities.label: How Much Can We Trust a Sample SD?

entities.description: Squared deviations make variance and SD sensitive to extreme values; the mean shifts too. Investigate the cause and measurement context. An unusual result may be real and must not be deleted solely because it changes the summaries.
entities.label: One Extreme Value Changes Everything

entities.description: Original
entities.label: v29 a1

entities.description: Modified
entities.label: v29 b1

entities.description: Illustrative comparison on the same unshifted concentration scale.
entities.label: Before and after one extreme value

entities.description: Illustrative change to QC Method A: replace only 10.2 with 15.2 mg/L. The original dataset is preserved.
entities.label: v29 context

entities.description: Synthetic teaching modification of QC Method A: only its final value changes from 10.2 to 15.2 mg/L. No published observations are changed.
entities.label: v29 data
Same observations, nested full-rank OLS models
One extra coefficient, one numerator degree of freedom

entities.description: Lowercase f is the observed unitless ratio; approximately equals marks rounded RSS inputs and a rounded result. Simple and complex RSS are 0.581971 and 0.064939 in squared response units. One added quadratic coefficient gives 3 minus 2 equals one numerator df; twelve observations minus three fitted coefficients leave nine denominator df. Under the null the added-term and complex-residual quadratic forms are independent; the two RSS values themselves are not.
entities.label: v3 calculation symbol

entities.description: Same twelve observations and residual scale. Compare linear and quadratic residuals before testing the added coefficient. A lower residual sum of squares is necessary, not sufficient justification.
entities.label: Does adding curvature remove the residual pattern?

entities.description: X is a random nitrate result; lowercase x is one concrete value, here 10.20 mg/L. The model expectation mu is 10.00 mg/L and its known positive SD sigma is 0.10 mg/L. Normal N uses mean and variance, so sigma squared has (mg/L) squared units. Uppercase Z is the standardized random variable with mean zero and variance one. Lowercase z is the concrete dimensionless z-score, here two. Subtract the expectation, then divide by SD; mg/L units cancel. Tilde names the distribution; equals defines or evaluates, minus subtracts, the fraction divides and the exponent squares. Standardizing a nonnormal variable does not make it normal.
entities.label: v3 eta symbol

entities.description: Six cancellation routes
entities.label: v3 four center

entities.description: Four signs in acquisition order: ++++ gives one extreme route. Zero has six routes: ++--, +-+-, +--+, -++-, -+-+, --++. Each sign adds or subtracts the same amount. The central mass is six of sixteen, not one combination.
entities.label: One extreme route versus six cancellation routes

entities.description: Where is 10.20 mg/L relative to expectation 10.00 and known SD 0.10 mg/L? It is two SD above the expectation. How often should that happen? Keep this probability question open.
entities.label: First locate the result in known SD units

entities.description: Can one stable normal model describe these results? Compare stable acquisition, one added outlier and drift on a common concentration window. No test decision is needed here.
entities.label: Inspect acquisition order before choosing a probability model
Five fixed categories, four count directions

entities.description: q is the observed unitless Pearson statistic, whose approximate null reference is chi-square with four df. Index j runs over the five fixed diameter categories; O and E are observed and expected counts, not concentrations. In the first category O is 4 and E is 10. Subtract, square the discrepancy, divide by the positive expected count and sum all five contributions. Equals gives the calculation; plus adds contributions. The fixed total 100 removes one independent count direction; no category probabilities are fitted. Independent classifications, exhaustive prespecified categories and adequate expected counts are needed for this approximation.
entities.label: v3 pearson symbol

entities.description: The first five residuals sum to minus 0.10 mg/L. The sixth must be plus 0.10 mg/L to preserve the zero-sum constraint. Changing any of the first five forces compensation. This leaves five independent residual directions, not five mutually independent raw residuals.
entities.label: v3 residual explanation
Add the first five, then negate their sum

entities.description: With the route on slide 2. Separate teaching appointment; extend or split according to audience participation. Durations are planning estimates, not observed timings.
entities.label: Session I: Normal and lognormal models, slides 3–30

entities.description: A separate appointment from Session I. Split at the Student or F transition when needed; do not promise one 90-minute treatment of all 66 slides.
entities.label: Session II: Chi-square, Student and F, slides 31–59

entities.description: Separate follow-up appointment after the distribution constructions. Reserve time for audience predictions and input-source comparisons.
entities.label: Session III: Model checks and Monte Carlo, slides 60–66

entities.description: Normal N(0,1) has dimensionless mean zero and variance one. Positive sample and population SDs make the square root of S squared over sigma squared equal S over sigma. Divide numerator and denominator by the same positive scale: sigma cancels. Independence of Z and Q follows from iid normal sampling, not from cancellation alone.
entities.label: v3 t operation

entities.description: Move the sum of all other terms to the opposite side. This is an algebraic constraint, not an independence assumption.
entities.label: Isolate one term of a zero sum

entities.description: a is the sum of the first five residuals and b the sixth, both in mg/L. Zero is their total. Add, negate and equate as shown; the arrow means implies. No random independence is asserted.
entities.label: v3 zero sum symbol

entities.description: Same unit does not mean same scale: raw MAD and IQR are not interchangeable with SD. Normal-model scaling is assumption-dependent, not a universal conversion. Robust summaries reduce sensitivity to extremes; they do not establish that an observation is erroneous.
entities.label: Robust Measures of Spread

entities.description: Sample SD: square root of SS/(n − 1), centered on the mean (11 mg/L here). Squaring makes it sensitive to the extreme result.
entities.label: SD: 2.351 mg/L

entities.description: xᵢ: an observation; median(x) = 10 mg/L; | · |: absolute distance. Take the median of these distances. In R: mad(x, constant=1).
entities.label: Raw MAD: 0.100 mg/L

entities.description: Q₃ − Q₁ = 10.1 − 9.9 mg/L using R's default type-7 quartiles. It describes the width of the central half, not a standard deviation.
entities.label: IQR: 0.200 mg/L

entities.description: Default: 1.4826 × raw MAD = 0.14826 mg/L before rounding. This large-sample normal-consistency scaling is not a small-sample unbiasedness correction.
entities.label: R mad(): 0.148 mg/L

entities.description: Seven minutes: compare a synthetic modification with the original QC measurements. Keep both datasets and document the change.
entities.label: R Lab 3: Explore the Influence of Outliers

entities.description:
Seven minutes: compare mean, median, SD, IQR and both versions of MAD before and after replacing 10.2 with 15.2 mg/L. All reported results here are in mg/L.
Which summaries react most, and why? Does stability of MAD or IQR establish that the observation is wrong? Explain why investigation must precede any exclusion.
entities.label: v31 task

entities.description: Repeated independent samples of the same size from one population would generate a distribution of sample means. This sampling distribution differs from the distribution of individual observations. Three sample means only illustrate the idea; they do not estimate that distribution reliably.
entities.label: The Spread of Observations and Means

entities.description: Nine individual values versus one mean per sample. These three synthetic means are an illustration, not a simulated sampling distribution.
entities.label: Individual results versus sample means

entities.description: So far, we have described how individual measurements vary. Now we ask how the mean itself varies between independent samples. Each illustrative sample contains n = 3 individual values and yields exactly one mean; recalculating the same data does not create a new sample.
entities.label: v32 context

entities.description: Means of the three synthetic samples: 10, 11, 9 mg/L. Three means illustrate the idea, not a well-estimated sampling distribution.
entities.label: v32 means

entities.description: Nine synthetic values in three illustrative samples; sample membership is given in the companion table.
entities.label: v32 observations
Three values → one mean (all in mg/L)

entities.description: For independent, identically distributed observations with finite variance, the true SEM is σ/√n. Replacing σ by s estimates it. Observation spread and precision of a mean estimate are different; SEM alone is not a complete measurement uncertainty.
entities.label: Standard Error of the Mean

entities.description: Estimated SD of the distribution of sample means across repeated samples. True SEM = σ/√n; the hat marks the estimate using s. Units are the same as the observations.
entities.label: Estimated SE / SEM

entities.description: The sample SD describes individual results, not the variability of sample means. Neither s nor SEM alone is a complete uncertainty budget or a measure of systematic error.
entities.label: s: individual-observation spread

entities.description: The simple formula requires independent, identically distributed observations with finite variance. Which observations actually count as independent observations in n? Count relevant independent sampling units, not automatically every injection.
entities.label: n: independent observations

entities.description: Four times as many independent observations halve SE: √(4n) = 2√n. Averaging reduces random variation in the mean; it does not change the individual-result SD σ or remove a systematic error.
entities.label: More Measurements, Smaller Standard Error

entities.description:
SE = 2/√4 = 1 mg/L.
Assumed individual-observation SD: 2 mg/L.
entities.label: n = 4

entities.description:
SE = 2/√16 = 0.5 mg/L.
Same population SD, four times as many independent data.
entities.label: n = 16

entities.description:
SE = 2/√64 = 0.25 mg/L.
Again four times the sample size, half the SE.
entities.label: n = 64

entities.description: Theoretical SE = σ/√n with assumed σ = 2 mg/L throughout. These are model calculations, not simulated measurements.
entities.label: Fourfold sample size, half the SE

entities.description: Theoretical standard errors σ/sqrt(n) for independent identically distributed observations with assumed σ = 2 mg/L. Derived summaries, not individual measured observations.
entities.label: v34 data
Hold population SD σ = 2 mg/L fixed

entities.description: The simple SEM assumes iid observations with finite variance. Label error bars explicitly: SD and SEM answer different questions; RSD describes relative spread, not the uncertainty of the estimated mean.
entities.label: SD, SE and RSD: Three Different Questions

entities.description: How much do individual results vary? SS: sum of squared deviations about x̄; n: count of observations. Sample SD uses n − 1 residual df and has the original measurement unit.
entities.label: SD: individual observations

entities.description: How much would the sample mean vary across independent repetitions? s: sample SD; n: independent observations per sample. The estimate has the original unit; it is not individual-result dispersion.
entities.label: SE: repeated sample means

entities.description: How large is SD relative to the mean? s/|x̄| is dimensionless; ×100 reports percent. |x̄| is the nonzero mean magnitude. Interpretation needs a suitable ratio scale and a mean away from zero.
entities.label: RSD: spread relative to level

entities.description: μ is fixed and unknown. The interval varies across samples but is fixed once the data are observed. For iid normal observations, n > 1 and unknown variance, 95% refers to long-run coverage of the procedure—not a 95% probability for μ in this particular interval.
entities.label: Confidence Interval for the Mean

entities.description: α is the significance level of the corresponding two-sided test and nominal noncoverage rate. Confidence level = 1 − α. For 95%, α = 0.05, split as α/2 in each tail.
entities.label: α and confidence level

entities.description: The (1 − α/2) quantile of Student's t distribution. Residual degrees of freedom: n − 1, because the mean is estimated from the same n observations.
entities.label: t critical value and df

entities.description: s: sample SD; n: independent observations. The estimated SD of sample means, in measurement units. Multiply by t to obtain the margin.
entities.label: s/√n: estimated SEM

entities.description: x̄ is the observed sample mean. Subtract/add the margin for lower/upper endpoints targeting the population mean μ, not individual observations.
entities.label: x̄ and the endpoints

entities.description: Under iid normal sampling, this interval estimates μ. It is not a specification for individual results and does not include every systematic or calibration contribution to measurement uncertainty. Calculate with unrounded values; round only for reporting.
entities.label: Confidence Interval: Worked Analytical Example

entities.description: n = 5 repeats; x̄ = 10 mg/L; sample variance s² = 0.025 (mg/L)². Its square root gives s ≈ 0.1581 mg/L.
entities.label: QC A: sample summaries

entities.description: Estimated SEM = s/√5 ≈ 0.07071 mg/L. df = 4; α = 0.05 gives t* = t(0.975,4) ≈ 2.776. The t value is dimensionless.
entities.label: SE and critical t

entities.description: Margin t* × SEM ≈ 0.1963 mg/L. Subtract/add it to x̄ = 10 mg/L. Report endpoints to three decimals; intermediate labels here are rounded approximations.
entities.label: Margin → endpoints

entities.description: QC Method A: the two-sided ninety-five percent t interval is approximately ten plus or minus 0.1963 milligrams per litre, giving endpoints 9.804 and 10.196 milligrams per litre.
entities.label: v37 formula

entities.description: Seven minutes: calculate a two-sided 95% t interval manually, then compare t.test().
entities.label: R Lab 4: Confidence Intervals

entities.description:
Seven minutes: assuming iid normal QC repeats, calculate the mean, SD, SE and qt() critical value. Compare the manual 95% interval with t.test().
The width comparison holds s fixed for hypothetical independent sample sizes. New data can also change s. Copying the same values does not create independent evidence or justify a smaller SE.
entities.label: v38 task

entities.description: Compare sites, independent samples within a site, preparations within a sample, and instrumental repeats within a preparation. A lower-level repeat does not measure every higher-level source. Independent, additive variance components require an appropriate model; nesting alone does not establish them.
entities.label: Variability Occurs at Different Levels

entities.description: Each parent may have several children. The four boxes show levels, not four independent observations.
entities.label: A nested analytical workflow

entities.description: Between-site variation
entities.label: Sampling site

entities.description: Between samples within a site
entities.label: Independent sample

entities.description: Between preparations of a sample
entities.label: Sample preparation

entities.description: Instrumental replicates within a preparation
entities.label: Instrument repeat

entities.description: Same fifteen values as in Variables. Within-site spread compares three values at one site; between-site variation compares sites, for example their means. Observed differences do not identify causes: three values per site cannot separate sampling, preparation and instrument variance without a suitable experimental design.
entities.label: Lake Sampling: Within-Site and Between-Site Variation

entities.description: Three measurement replicates per site, on one common concentration axis. Their sampling/preparation independence is not established by the plot.
entities.label: Lake analyte A: the original fifteen values

entities.description: The number of measurements is not necessarily the number of independent experimental units. An independent unit supplies separate evidence for the target question under the design and assumptions. Pseudoreplication counts dependent or nested readings as if they were such units; the label ‘replicate’ does not establish independence.
entities.label: What Counts as an Independent Replicate?

entities.description: Technical replicates: repeated readings of the same material. Capture injection/instrument variation, not preparation or field-sampling variation. Shared drift can still cause dependence.
entities.label: Three injections, one vial

entities.description: Separately prepare aliquots of one sample. Can capture preparation plus downstream measurement variation. They share the field sample and are not three independent field units.
entities.label: Three independent preparations

entities.description: Separately collect, prepare and measure samples. Can capture sampling plus downstream variation. Independent evidence for a field target depends on spatial/temporal design and shared conditions.
entities.label: Three independent field samples

entities.description: For a linear model with a full-column-rank design matrix, residual df = n − p. Here p counts independent estimated model coefficients. This is a model-rank statement, not a universal formula for every statistical procedure.
entities.label: Degrees of Freedom Beyond the Mean

entities.description: X is the linear-model design matrix. For ordinary least squares, full column rank gives p independently estimable coefficients and p residual constraints. In general, residual df = n − rank(X).
entities.label: n observations, p estimable parameters

entities.description: p = 1: one intercept/mean. Residual df = n − 1.
entities.label: Estimate one mean

entities.description: p = 2: intercept and slope. With distinct x values and full rank, residual df = n − 2.
entities.label: Fit a straight line

entities.description: Illustrative UV/Vis calibration: five standards, two fitted coefficients, three residual df. OLS fit: intercept 0.044 a.u.; slope 0.982 a.u. per mg/L; SS residual = 0.01824 a.u.²; s_res ≈ 0.07797 a.u. It measures response scatter about the fitted line, not concentration uncertainty.
entities.label: Residual Standard Deviation in Calibration

entities.description: Only the fitted model is drawn. Endpoint markers are model predictions, not observations. Observed signals appear in the table: the current line-chart contract cannot show an unconnected observation series alongside the fitted line.
entities.label: OLS model: ŷ = 0.044 + 0.982x

entities.description: Illustrative UV/Vis calibration standards; concentrations 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 mg/L.
entities.label: Observed signals

entities.description: xᵢ: standard concentration; yᵢ: observed response; ŷᵢ: predicted response. β₀: intercept; β₁: slope; εᵢ: model error. n − 2: residual df. Interpreting s_res as an error SD assumes independent zero-mean errors of common variance and a suitable linear model.
entities.label: Model and residuals
Observed y, fitted ŷ and residual (a.u.)

entities.description: Six minutes: fit a calibration line with intercept and slope and inspect its residual spread.
entities.label: R Lab 5: Residual Degrees of Freedom

entities.description:
Six minutes: use lm(), coef(), residuals() and df.residual(). Check the manual residual SD against summary(fit)$sigma.
Why do fitting an intercept and slope leave only three residual df? Explain what this signal-scale SD describes and why it is not concentration uncertainty.
entities.label: v44 task

entities.description: Discuss two QC methods using five repeats each. The inclusive interval [9.5, 10.5] mg/L is an illustrative teaching rule, not a validated routine-performance requirement. These results alone cannot establish routine suitability.
entities.label: Analytical Decision Challenge

entities.label: v45 a1

entities.label: v45 b1

Discuss in pairs: what would you report about A versus B from these five results each? Compare means, SD, RSD and counts in the inclusive illustrative interval [9.5, 10.5] mg/L.
Which measurement conditions and independent sampling units must be known? Propose further independent replication and a validated performance requirement before judging routine suitability. Separate what n = 5 shows from what it cannot establish.

entities.description: The mean describes location; variance describes spread.
entities.label: v46 k1

entities.description: Variance has squared units; SD is its square root, in the original unit.
entities.label: v46 k2

entities.description: Degrees of freedom account for constraints introduced by estimated parameters.

entities.description: SD: individual spread. SE: sampling spread of an estimate. RSD: SD relative to |mean|.

entities.description: Do not force every variable into one mutually exclusive hierarchy. Instead ask several independent questions about its values and scale.
entities.label: variable classification intro

entities.description: These classifications describe the values and the mathematics that can be applied to them. They do not tell us whether the variable is modeled as random.
entities.label: variable classification takeaway

entities.description: A variable is allowed to change within the stated scope; a constant is treated as fixed within that scope. The distinction is contextual rather than an intrinsic property of a physical quantity: a wavelength can be constant in one experiment and deliberately varied in another.
entities.label: variable constant comparison

entities.description: Whether a quantity is a variable or a constant depends on the scope and design of the experiment or dataset. Calling a quantity constant means it is treated as fixed for the current analysis, not that it can never change in another context.
entities.label: variable constant scope interpretation

entities.description:
CAN CHANGE
Values may differ across observations, samples or experimental conditions.
entities.label: variable keypoint change

entities.description:
HAS A ROLE
A variable can be measured, deliberately controlled or used in a model.
entities.label: variable keypoint role

entities.description:
NEEDS A SCOPE
The same physical quantity can be variable in one study and constant in another.
entities.label: variable keypoint scope

entities.description: A variable is useful only when its role and scope are explicit.

entities.description: A variable specifies what can take different values. A concrete measurement gives one observed value x_i. Several observations together form a statistical sample.

entities.description: Precision is closeness of agreement among repeated measurement results under stated conditions. A standard deviation quantifies the spread of such results, but it must be associated with a specified measurand, procedure and measurement conditions.
entities.label: What Does SD Tell Us About Precision?

entities.description: Closeness of agreement among repeated measurement results under stated conditions.
entities.label: Precision

entities.description: Smaller SD means less observed spread. Precision depends on stated measurement conditions.
entities.label: Standard deviation

entities.description: Scenario: five QC determinations in one morning. Same procedure, operator, instrument and laboratory over a short interval. The SD describes repeatability for this procedure and material.
entities.label: Repeatability

entities.description: Scenario: one laboratory measures the same QC material over several days, with specified operator changes. The SD includes variation under these within-laboratory changes.
entities.label: Intermediate precision

entities.description: Scenario: different laboratories analyze the same homogeneous QC material using a specified procedure. Their results assess between-laboratory conditions. These labels do not imply a universal ordering of SDs.
entities.label: Reproducibility
Repeated Measurements of a Control Sample

entities.description: Five repeats per method on the same control sample under fixed repeatability conditions.
entities.label: vr28a

entities.description: A has smaller observed SD. Five repeats provide limited evidence about long-term performance.
entities.label: vr28b
Why Precision Alone Is Not Enough

entities.description: Closeness of the long-run mean result to a reference value. A small SD alone does not establish trueness.
entities.label: Trueness

entities.description: Long-run mean result minus the reference value. A tightly clustered set of results can still have an offset.
entities.label: Bias

entities.description: Requires relevant performance requirements and measurement conditions, not only a small observed SD.
entities.label: Method suitability
What Counts as an Independent Replicate?

entities.description: Inject one prepared vial three times. These technical replicates assess instrumental variation, not new preparation or field sampling. Shared drift may still make the readings dependent.
entities.label: Three injections, one vial

entities.description: Prepare three aliquots of one field sample separately and measure each. This captures preparation plus downstream variation. They share the field sample; independent preparation errors require justified assumptions about common batch effects. They are not three field units.
entities.label: Three independent preparations

entities.description: Collect, prepare and measure three field samples separately. These may be independent experimental units for a field question, depending on spatial and temporal design. Pseudoreplication counts nested readings as separate field units.
entities.label: Three independent field samples

entities.description: Repeating only instrument readings misses earlier sources of variation.
entities.label: Repeat the relevant steps

entities.description: Nesting does not establish independent, additive variance components. That requires a model.
entities.label: Separate design from model

entities.description: Repeating only instrument readings misses earlier sources of variation.
entities.label: vr31a

entities.description: Nesting does not establish independent, additive variance components. That requires a model.
entities.label: vr31b

entities.description: Within-site spread and differences between site means are different comparisons.
entities.label: vr32a

entities.description: Three values per site cannot separate sampling, preparation and instrument causes without a suitable design.
entities.label: vr32b

entities.description: Both means are 10 mg/L. SD and RSD give the same ranking here.
entities.label: vr34a

entities.description: RSD reports relative spread, not trueness or guaranteed future performance.
entities.label: vr34b

entities.description: RSD is undefined at a zero mean and unstable near zero. Blank measurements need absolute-spread assessment.
entities.label: vr35a

entities.description: Ratios need a meaningful zero. RSD of Celsius temperatures is inappropriate.
entities.label: vr35b
The Influence of an Extreme Measurement

entities.description: Replace only QC A's 10.2 with 15.2 mg/L. The mean, variance and SD all increase.
entities.label: vr36a

entities.description: Investigate the cause. A large effect on the summaries is not a reason for automatic deletion.

entities.description: Superscript 2 means square. Multiplying dᵢ + Δ by itself gives a residual square, two equal cross-products and the offset square. Every term has squared measurement units.

entities.description: Xᵢ: observation i; i: index; n: count greater than 1. dᵢ: residual about the sample mean. Δ: sample mean minus population mean μ.
entities.label: Random quantities

entities.description: E: repeated-sampling expectation. σ²: population variance. Σ sums from i = 1 to n. Superscript 2 means square. MSDₙ: sum of squared residuals divided by n. Here σ² = 5 (mg/L)².

entities.description: Independent identical sampling with finite variance gives E[nΔ²] = σ². Subtract this from nσ² to get the expected residual sum of squares; divide by n for expected MSD. Normality is not required.

entities.description: σ²: expected squared distance from μ. Superscript 2 means square. Its unit is (mg/L)² when X has unit mg/L.

accessibility.label: Variance and Uncertainty of the Mean

blocks.text: Variance and Uncertainty of the Mean

scenes.narration: A mean describes a center, but not the variation around that center. This lecture develops measures of spread from observed residuals, explains why estimating the mean changes variance estimation, and connects variation of sample means to random uncertainty. The practical interpretation always depends on what was measured and which sampling assumptions are justified.

accessibility.label: Same Mean, Different Spread

blocks.text: Same Mean, Different Spread

items.text: Scenario: compare measurement series A and B.
Their arithmetic means are the same: 32/3 mg/L.
Do they show the same measurement behavior?

blocks.description: Each dot is one observation. Both means are 32/3 mg/L, approximately 10.667 mg/L.
blocks.label: Same mean, different spread

scenes.narration:
The measurement series 9, 10 and 13 mg/L and 5, 10 and 17 mg/L have the same arithmetic mean, $32/3$ mg/L. The second series is much more dispersed.

A report containing only their common mean would conceal this difference. We therefore need a quantity that describes the distances between the observations and their center.

accessibility.label: Why Does Spread Matter in the Laboratory?

blocks.text: Why Does Spread Matter in the Laboratory?

items.text: Scenario: two analytical methods measure the same control sample.
Both give results around the target, with different variability.
Would one method be preferable?

blocks.description: Five illustrative repeats per method. These are QC Methods A/B, not the three-observation Series A/B.
blocks.label: Control sample: assigned target 10 mg/L

scenes.narration: Spread matters when judging agreement among repeated laboratory measurements. A tightly clustered series and a widely scattered series can have similar means while supporting different statements about repeatability. Such comparisons require consistent units and stated measurement conditions. An illustrative target interval helps discuss results, but it is not automatically a validated analytical acceptance requirement.

The plotted stems show signed distances from each observation to that fitted mean. Series A is more tightly clustered than Series B. No population mean or population variance has been measured merely by computing this shared sample center.

Residuals retain the measurement unit and indicate both direction and distance: negative values fall below the fitted mean, and positive values above it. blocks.spokenText: Mathematische Formel für squared deviation

entries.description: xᵢ: observation i; i: index; x̄: sample mean; dᵢ: their signed difference. Superscript 2 denotes squaring.
n: observation count; Σ: sum from 1 to n. SS adds the squared deviations. Squaring mg/L produces the unit (mg/L)².

items.text: Squared deviations do not cancel and therefore preserve information about spread.

scenes.narration:
Squaring each residual makes every contribution nonnegative, so opposite signs no longer cancel. The sum of squared residuals increases when observations lie farther from their fitted center.

Its unit is the square of the measurement unit, here $(\mathrm{mg/L})^2$. Because the total also depends on the number of contributions, we next normalize it by the sample size.

items.text: MSD describes the average squared deviation per observation.

scenes.narration: The mean squared deviation, MSD, is the sum of squared residuals divided by the number of observations. It is a descriptive summary of this particular sample around its own fitted mean. Series A and Series B have the same center, but different MSD values. Describing the observed sample and estimating an unknown population variance are related tasks, not identical definitions.
